articles.title: The city closing down streets so children can play
articles.summary: In Leeds, streets are being temporarily closed to traffic so kids have more space to safely play - an initiative proving beneficial to both children and adults.
articles.content:
Seven-year-old Aydin is relishing the chance to play somewhere new. It's Colenso Mount, a street in the Holbeck area of Leeds where he lives, which has been temporarily closed to traffic to become a ‘Play Street’.

"Everyone can ride scooters and the boys over there play football which is very fun", he says excitedly.

As Aydin jumps a scooter over ramps set up in the middle of the road, children around him are drawing with chalk, blowing bubbles and kicking a football in a spot where cars are usually driving through.

It’s a rare chance for the kids in this neighbourhood to play outside together, in a space big enough to frolic and safe from traffic.

According to a survey from the campaign group Play Their Way, external, out on Wednesday, nearly half of parents (46%) say their child doesn't have a safe place to play outdoors.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being urged to bring back a national play strategy, external for children in England - an initiative he championed while culture secretary in 2008.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful community initiative where streets are temporarily closed to create safe play spaces for children, addressing a widespread issue of lack of safe outdoor play areas. This has positive social impact by promoting child wellbeing and community engagement, with potential for broader policy influence.
articles.personality_title: Leeds closes streets temporarily to create safe play areas for children
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many children in England do not have safe outdoor spaces to play. In Leeds, this problem is being addressed by turning some streets into temporary play areas.

**What happened** – In the Holbeck area of Leeds, a street called Colenso Mount has been closed to traffic for a short time, allowing children like seven-year-old Aydin to play safely outside. Kids are riding scooters, playing football, drawing with chalk, and blowing bubbles on the street, which is usually busy with cars.

**Impact** – This change gives children a rare chance to play together in a large, safe space near their homes. It also brings the community together and shows how simple changes can improve children’s wellbeing. Almost half of parents say their children lack safe places to play, so this idea could help many families.

**What's next step** – There is a call for a national plan to create more safe play spaces across England. The government is being encouraged to support such initiatives, which could lead to more streets being closed temporarily for children’s play in other areas.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Closing streets temporarily in Leeds creates safe, fun places for children to play and could inspire wider efforts to provide outdoor play spaces across England.

articles.personality_title_es: Leeds cierra calles temporalmente para crear áreas de juego seguras para niños
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos niños en Inglaterra no tienen espacios al aire libre seguros para jugar. En Leeds, están abordando este problema convirtiendo algunas calles en áreas de juego temporales.

Los niños montan patinetas, juegan fútbol, dibujan con tiza y soplan burbujas en la calle, que normalmente está llena de autos.

**Impacto** – Este cambio ofrece a los niños una oportunidad rara de jugar juntos en un espacio grande y seguro cerca de sus casas. También une a la comunidad y muestra cómo cambios simples pueden mejorar el bienestar de los niños. Casi la mitad de los padres dicen que a sus hijos les falta un lugar seguro para jugar, por lo que esta idea podría ayudar a muchas familias.

**Próximo paso** – Se está pidiendo un plan nacional para crear más espacios de juego seguros en toda Inglaterra. Se anima al gobierno a apoyar estas iniciativas, lo que podría llevar a cerrar temporalmente más calles para que los niños jueguen en otras áreas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Cerrar calles temporalmente en Leeds crea lugares seguros y divertidos para que los niños jueguen y podría inspirar esfuerzos más amplios para proporcionar espacios al aire libre para jugar en Inglaterra.

articles.title: The cost of being single – and how friends are teaming up to beat it
articles.summary: Many singles face extra costs for housing, bills, food and holidays but there are ways to ease the burden.
articles.content:
When Leanne split up with her partner in her late 20s she thought she'd have to put her dream of a buying a home in the area where she grew up on hold.

She was earning a good salary but the properties she was hoping for - with a garden and parking space - were too expensive on her own. While she'd just started seeing someone new, it was very early days - far too early to discuss living together.

Her friend since school, Sarah, was single and renting a room in a shared house in Brighton. She also wanted to move back home to Kent, but was worried about how she'd get on the housing ladder on her cabin crew salary.

When Sarah suggested they buy together, Leanne admits she "totally baulked". But after chatting with a mortgage adviser they went ahead - and say it's helped them avoid the so-called singles tax.

Not being partnered up can mean extra costs. It's tricky to quantify and varies by location - estimates suggest it could be anything from hundreds of pounds to £10,000 on average extra, external a year.

The cost of rent or a mortgage, household bills and subscriptions can't be shared. And a single person pays 25% less council tax than a couple - not half.

Many discounts involve pairing up - 2-for-1 cinema tickets, Two-Together railcards, couples gym memberships - plus solo travellers often pay a single person supplement.

This affects a lot of people. Some 18.5m people had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2024 – 36.8% of the population aged 16 and over, official figures show.

And overall 8.6m people were estimated to be living alone in the UK last year - that's nearly a third of all households.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant social issue affecting a large portion of the population—extra financial burdens faced by single people—and presents a practical, community-based solution where friends team up to overcome these challenges. This has broad societal relevance and offers a hopeful, actionable approach to improving quality of life for many individuals.
articles.personality_title: Friends team up to share home costs and beat the 'single tax'
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many single people face higher costs for housing, bills, and activities because prices are often designed for couples or families. This extra expense is sometimes called the "single tax." For example, singles often pay more for rent, utilities, and miss out on discounts made for two or more people.

**What happened** – Leanne and Sarah, two single friends, decided to buy a home together after realizing it was too expensive to do alone. Leanne recently separated from her partner and wanted to buy a house with a garden and parking near where she grew up. Sarah also wanted to move back home but worried about affording a place on her cabin crew salary. After talking to a mortgage adviser, they teamed up to buy a house, sharing costs and responsibilities.

**Impact** – This approach helped them avoid the extra costs singles usually face. By sharing a home, they split mortgage payments, bills, and other expenses, making it more affordable. Their story shows a practical way to handle financial challenges that affect millions of single people in the UK, where nearly a third of households are single-person homes.

**What's next step** – More singles might consider teaming up with friends or trusted people to share housing and reduce costs. This could lead to new types of home-sharing arrangements and financial advice focused on helping singles find affordable living options.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Two single friends bought a home together to share costs and avoid the extra expenses many singles face living alone.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des amis s'associent pour partager les frais de logement et éviter la « taxe des célibataires »
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de personnes célibataires ont des coûts plus élevés pour le logement, les factures et les activités car les prix sont souvent pensés pour les couples ou les familles. Ce surplus de dépenses est parfois appelé la « taxe des célibataires ». Par exemple, les célibataires paient souvent plus pour le loyer, les services publics, et ne bénéficient pas des réductions pour deux personnes ou plus.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Leanne et Sarah, deux amies célibataires, ont décidé d’acheter une maison ensemble après avoir réalisé que c’était trop cher seules. Leanne venait de se séparer et voulait acheter une maison avec jardin et parking près de son lieu d’enfance. Sarah voulait aussi revenir chez elle mais s’inquiétait de pouvoir payer avec son salaire d’hôtesse de l’air. Après avoir parlé à un conseiller en prêt immobilier, elles ont acheté la maison à deux, partageant les coûts et responsabilités.

**Impact** – Cette solution leur a permis d’éviter les coûts supplémentaires que subissent les célibataires. En partageant la maison, elles divisent les paiements du prêt, les factures et autres dépenses, ce qui rend tout plus abordable. Leur histoire montre une façon pratique de gérer les difficultés financières qui touchent des millions de célibataires au Royaume-Uni, où près d’un tiers des ménages sont composés d’une seule personne.

**Étape suivante** – D’autres célibataires pourraient envisager de s’associer avec des amis ou des personnes de confiance pour partager un logement et réduire les coûts. Cela pourrait ouvrir la voie à de nouvelles formes de colocation et de conseils financiers adaptés aux célibataires.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Deux amies célibataires ont acheté une maison ensemble pour partager les dépenses et éviter les coûts supplémentaires auxquels font face beaucoup de célibataires vivant seuls.
articles.personality_title_es: Amigos se unen para compartir gastos de vivienda y evitar el 'impuesto para solteros'
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas solteras enfrentan costos más altos por vivienda, facturas y actividades porque los precios suelen estar diseñados para parejas o familias. Este gasto extra a veces se llama el "impuesto para solteros". Por ejemplo, los solteros suelen pagar más por el alquiler, los servicios y no reciben descuentos pensados para dos o más personas.

**Qué pasó** – Leanne y Sarah, dos amigas solteras, decidieron comprar una casa juntas tras darse cuenta de que era muy caro hacerlo solas. Leanne se había separado recientemente y quería comprar una casa con jardín y estacionamiento cerca de donde creció. Sarah también quería regresar a su ciudad natal, pero estaba preocupada por poder pagar una vivienda con su sueldo de tripulante de cabina. Después de hablar con un asesor hipotecario, se unieron para comprar la casa, compartiendo costos y responsabilidades.

**Impacto** – Esta idea les ayudó a evitar los gastos extra que suelen tener los solteros. Compartiendo la vivienda, dividen los pagos de la hipoteca, las facturas y otros gastos, haciéndolo más asequible. Su historia muestra una forma práctica de enfrentar los retos financieros que afectan a millones de solteros en el Reino Unido, donde casi un tercio de los hogares son de una sola persona.

**Próximo paso** – Más solteros podrían considerar unirse con amigos o personas de confianza para compartir vivienda y reducir costos. Esto podría llevar a nuevas formas de convivencia y consejos financieros para ayudar a los solteros a encontrar opciones de vida más asequibles.

**Resumen en una frase** – Dos amigas solteras compraron una casa juntas para compartir gastos y evitar los costos extra que enfrentan muchos solteros que viven solos.
